title: Easy exam 13
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: find actions, aliases, grouping commands, regular expressions on a word list, initrd, case sensitivity, foreground jobs, exit statuses, deleting files and read.

questions.title: The actions of find
questions.text: Which statement about `find` actions is FALSE?

options.t: `find . -name '*.tmp' -exec rm {} \;` runs `rm` once for each file found.
options.why: True: `{}` is replaced by the name of each file.

options.t: `find . -name '*.log' -exec ls -l {} +` passes many file names to a single `ls`.
options.why: True: with `+` the names are grouped, as `xargs` does.

options.t: `find . -name '*.tmp' -delete` removes every file that matches.
options.why: True.

options.t: `find . -name '*.tmp' -delete` asks for confirmation before removing each file.
options.why: False: `-delete` removes at once, without asking; the action that asks is `-ok`.

questions.title: What an alias does
questions.text: After typing `alias hi='echo hello'` in an interactive shell, what does `hi world` print?

options.t: `hello world`
options.why: The shell replaces the word `hi` by `echo hello` and keeps the rest of the line.

options.t: `hi: command not found`
options.why: The alias is known by the shell, so `hi` is replaced before the shell looks for a command.

options.t: `world`
options.why: Only the alias name is replaced; the arguments stay in the line and `echo` prints them.

options.t: `hello`
options.why: The arguments written after the alias are not lost: they are appended to the expansion.

questions.title: One redirection for two commands
questions.text: Which command writes the output of both `echo one` and `echo two` into the file `out.txt`?

options.t: `{ echo one; echo two; } > out.txt`
options.why: The braces group the commands, and the redirection applies to the output of the whole group.

options.t: `echo one; echo two > out.txt`
options.why: Only `echo two` is redirected; `one` goes to the screen.

options.t: `echo one | echo two > out.txt`
options.why: `echo` ignores its input: the file contains only `two`.

options.t: `echo one && echo two > out.txt`
options.why: The redirection still affects only the second command.

questions.title: Matching words
questions.text: In a list of English words, which statement about `grep '^c.t$' words` is TRUE?

options.t: It prints the three-letter words that start with `c` and end with `t`, such as `cat` or `cut`.
options.why: `^` and `$` fix the start and the end of the line, and the dot stands for exactly one character.

options.t: It prints the words that contain the text `c.t` with a real dot.
options.why: To search for a literal dot it must be written `\.`.

options.t: It prints every word that starts with `c` or ends with `t`.
options.why: The pattern requires both conditions and exactly one letter between them.

options.t: It prints words of any length that start with `c` and end with `t`, such as `cart`.
options.why: The dot matches one character, so `cart` (two letters between `c` and `t`) does not match.

questions.title: Kernel messages at boot
questions.text: Which command shows the messages that the kernel printed while the system was starting?

options.t: `dmesg`
options.why: It prints the kernel ring buffer: hardware detection, drivers loaded, the root file system being mounted...

options.t: `last`
options.why: It lists the past logins of the users, read from `/var/log/wtmp`.

options.t: `history`
options.why: It lists the commands typed in the current shell.

options.t: `uname -a`
options.why: It prints the name and version of the kernel, not the messages it wrote.

questions.title: Names in any case
questions.text: Linux treats `Notes.TXT` and `notes.txt` as different files. Which command lists both?

options.t: `find . -iname notes.txt`
options.why: `-iname` ignores the difference between upper and lower case in the name.

options.t: `find . -name notes.txt`
options.why: `-name` is case sensitive: it finds only `notes.txt`.

options.t: `find . -name 'notes.TXT'`
options.why: It finds only the file with exactly that spelling.

options.t: `find . -name notes.txt -i`
options.why: `-i` is not an option of `find`; it fails with "unknown predicate".

questions.title: Foreground jobs
questions.text: Which statement defines a foreground job?

options.t: The job that owns the terminal: the shell waits for it before the next prompt.
options.why: Only one job at a time can be in the foreground; `Ctrl+C` and `Ctrl+Z` act on it.

options.t: A job that runs with a higher priority than the others.
options.why: Foreground and background say nothing about priority.

options.t: A job that has no terminal and is started at boot.
options.why: That describes a daemon.

options.t: A job that keeps running after the user logs out.
options.why: That is what `nohup` is for.

options.t: Only when `cmd1` fails, that is, ends with a status different from 0.
options.why: `||` means "or else": the second command is a fallback.

options.t: Only when `cmd1` succeeds.
options.why: That is what `&&` does.

options.t: Always, after `cmd1` has finished.
options.why: That is what `;` does.

options.t: At the same time as `cmd1`, in the background.
options.why: Running at the same time is what `&` or a pipe does.

questions.title: Deleting needs the directory
questions.text: Which statement about deleting the file `docs/old.txt` is FALSE?

options.t: To delete it you need write and execute permission on the directory `docs`.
options.why: True: deleting changes the directory, which lists the names.

options.t: A file with mode `r--r--r--` can be deleted if you have write permission on its directory.
options.why: True: the permissions of the file are not consulted.

options.t: If `docs` has mode `r-xr-xr-x` you cannot delete the file, even if you own it.
options.why: True: nobody has write permission on the directory.

options.t: You can delete it only if you have write permission on the file itself.
options.why: False: the permission that matters is the one of the directory that contains the name.

questions.title: The read command
questions.text: What does `read -p "Name: " n` do in a script?

options.t: It prints the prompt `Name: ` and stores the typed line in the variable `n`.
options.why: `-p` gives the prompt text and the first word after the options is the variable that receives the input.

options.t: It reads the content of a file called `Name: ` into the variable `n`.
options.why: `read` reads standard input, not a file named by `-p`.

options.t: It prints `Name: ` and the value of `n`.
options.why: It does not print the variable; it assigns it.

options.t: It pipes the output of the previous command into `n`.
options.why: `-p` has nothing to do with pipes.
